practices.claim: Give Claude a runnable check (tests, build, linter) and have it iterate until the check passes.
practices.check: Read the share of editing sessions that ran a test/build/lint/typecheck after the last edit. A low share is a gap only for sessions where a check existed; do not call doc-only or config edits a miss.
practices.notes: Docs: 'the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from' (date shown is the fetch date; docs are undated). Anthropic's June 2026 expertise study links expertise to 'verified success', but the link is correlational and partly circular. Corroborated by Karpathy's field notes (section VI: a success criterion defined before coding; https://gist.github.com/DiTo97/e734f688f6f63fc45211142c0e43d307; opinion, not measured).

practices.claim: Have Claude show command output as evidence rather than just claiming it worked.
practices.check: No metric checks this; a sample reader can look at whether final messages quote check output.
practices.notes: Docs advice, no data.

practices.claim: Tell Claude in the prompt or CLAUDE.md to verify its own work before it finishes.
practices.check: A gap only when transcripts show changes reported done with no test or build output. Never apply this on Opus 5; see avoid-verification-boilerplate-opus-5.
practices.notes: Prompting best practices: 'Ask Claude to self-check… catches errors reliably… Claude Opus 5 is the exception'. The Sonnet 5.5 page says to add a verification paragraph 'If you see changes reported as complete without test or build output in the transcript'. The docs name only Opus 5 as the exception; nobody knows whether that covers Opus 5.5. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

practices.claim: On Opus 5, remove carried-over 'verify your work' instructions; they cause over-verification (extra tokens and latency).
practices.check: A hard check (test, hook) is still good; look for the same check re-run several times with no edit between, not for a low verification rate. Never read few verify phrases in prompts as a gap.
practices.notes: Docs: 'verification instructions carried over… can cause over-verification, adding tokens and latency… remove these instructions'. Thariq Shihipar, 2026-09-29 (x.com/trq212/status/2104983034152063339): 'Smart models need less verification which makes them pareto dominant.'

practices.claim: After a long unattended run, have a fresh subagent review the diff before you count the work done.
practices.check: Read sessions with 20+ edits and no human message, and how many had a review after. A gap only when an unreviewed run later needed fixes: corrections or reverts of that work in the transcripts. Skip Opus 5 sessions.
practices.notes: Best-practices, 'Add an adversarial review step': 'The longer Claude works unattended, the more an independent check matters before you count the work as done.' The same section warns that a reviewer will report gaps even in sound work; act only on gaps that affect correctness. The Opus 5 prompting page says 'do not use subagents to verify or double-check your own work', so Opus 5 is excluded; nobody knows whether that covers Opus 5.5. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

suggest.name: /code-review
suggest.what: Reviews the current diff for bugs in a fresh subagent.

suggest.name: /security-review
suggest.what: Reviews your branch's changes for security holes.

practices.claim: Use plan mode (explore, plan, then code) for multi-file or uncertain work; skip it if you could describe the diff in one sentence.
practices.check: Never a gap. Plan-mode use, high or low, describes the person's habits; do not grade it.
practices.notes: The docs still recommend it. Best-practices: 'Explore first, then plan, then code'; plan mode 'adds overhead', and 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.' Costs: 'Use plan mode for complex tasks'. Superseded because newer first-hand staff posts say current models rarely need it. Expertise study: users make about 70% of planning decisions, correlated with success (correlational). Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

practices.claim: Start most sessions in plan mode.
practices.check: Never a gap. Boris and Thariq have since moved away from plan mode.
practices.notes: Source is secondary (paddo.dev); x.com was not fetched directly for this post. Kept because the later first-hand posts reverse it.

practices.claim: Use auto mode, and plan only when the task needs it; current models rarely need plan mode.
practices.check: The plan-mode count describes the person's habits; it does not grade them. Never flag plan-mode use, high or low, as a gap.
practices.notes: Boris 2026-05-22: 'my #1 tip is: use auto mode'. Boris 2026-06-08 (status/2064034799711588805) gives 'why I use auto mode instead of plan mode'. Thariq 2026-09-23 (x.com/trq212/status/2102813194196758746): 'thinking of killing plan mode… I don't think the models need plan mode anymore'. These posts are newer than the docs and outweigh them. Staff experience, no data. x.com returns 402, so the quotes were not re-checked. In the docs, plan mode also uses the auto classifier: both are values of one permission-mode setting.

practices.claim: Write prompts that name files, constraints, existing patterns, the symptom and what 'fixed' looks like.
practices.check: A high correction rate may reflect vague prompts, but it also reflects hard tasks and model changes; use samples to judge, never the rate alone.
practices.notes: Costs doc: vague requests 'trigger broad scanning'. Economic Index (2026-01-15) shows prompt and response sophistication correlate; no causal claim. Corroborated by Karpathy's field notes (section VI Goal-Driven Execution: define a verifiable success criterion before coding and state the plan for multi-step work so a wrong approach is caught early; https://gist.github.com/DiTo97/e734f688f6f63fc45211142c0e43d307; opinion, not measured).

practices.claim: On Opus 5 and Sonnet 5.5, state the task's scope and tell Claude not to add work you did not ask for.
practices.check: No metric. Read it only from the sample readers' out_of_scope cause, never from the number of changed files. A gap only when samples show the person rejecting or reverting work they did not ask for.
practices.notes: Opus 5 page: the model 'can also expand the scope of a task, adding steps that weren't requested or applying its own judgment about what the task should be.' Sonnet 5.5 page (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-sonnet-5-5): it 'tends to add tests, documentation, and small supporting files' unasked, more at higher effort, and 'Most teams will welcome this.' Both pages give a prompt that limits scope. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated. Corroborated by Karpathy's field notes (https://gist.github.com/DiTo97/e734f688f6f63fc45211142c0e43d307, section X 'Kitchen Sink' and 'Runaway Refactor'; opinion, not measured).

practices.claim: Keep CLAUDE.md short: cut every line Claude would not miss, and move occasional workflows into skills.
practices.check: Read loaded lines as a hint. 'Under 200 lines' is a heuristic, not a fail line. A gap only when transcripts show Claude ignoring a rule the file states.
practices.notes: Best-practices: 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, cut it.' and 'Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!' The costs doc adds 'Aim to keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines'. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

suggest.name: /context
suggest.what: Shows what fills the context window and flags memory bloat.

suggest.name: /doctor
suggest.what: Proposes cuts for CLAUDE.md content Claude can derive from the code.

practices.claim: Keep only context-file lines that earn their cost: in a benchmark, LLM-written files raised cost over 20% and developer-written ones gave no significant gain.
practices.check: Supports pruning. The data is SWE-bench-style tasks on Sonnet 4.5-era models; never apply the 20% figure to this person's own sessions.
practices.notes: Paper v3 (revised 2026-09-29): developer-written files raised success by 2.4% on average, p=0.21, not significant. The over-20% cost rise is for LLM-generated files. Title: Evaluating AGENTS.md. Figures read through a summarizer, so close but not verbatim.

practices.claim: After a correction, have Claude add a rule to CLAUDE.md so the mistake does not repeat, and prune the file ruthlessly.
practices.check: Growth alone is not a gap. A gap only when the same correction repeats across sessions, whether the file grew or not.
practices.notes: Boris: 'Ruthlessly edit your CLAUDE.md over time. Keep iterating until Claude's mistake rate measurably drops.' The post also says to prune, so it fits the short-file advice. x.com returns 402, so the quote was not re-checked.

practices.claim: Use /clear between unrelated tasks instead of one long kitchen-sink session.
practices.check: Compare /clear counts and sessions with 2+ compactions. Long sessions on one topic are fine; do not count them as a gap.
practices.notes: Costs doc calls clearing between tasks and matching the model to the job the highest-impact habits. Docs also say 'Sometimes you should let context accumulate'.

practices.claim: Models get less reliable as the input grows, even on simple tasks.
practices.check: Use only as background for long sessions. It was measured on 18 models in isolated tasks, not on agentic Claude Code sessions or current models.
practices.notes: Anthropic's context engineering post (2025-09-29) cites it.

practices.claim: After two failed corrections on the same issue, /clear and re-prompt instead of correcting a third time.
practices.check: Count sessions with 2+ consecutive corrections and read samples to see whether it was the same issue. A streak is not always a failure: the task may simply be iterative.
practices.notes: Docs: 'A clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections'. No data.

practices.claim: Stop Claude with Esc, or /rewind, as soon as it goes off track instead of letting a bad path run.
practices.check: Read interrupts and rewinds per session. A gap only when samples show Claude running long on a wrong path that the person corrected late. Zero interrupts with few corrections is fine.
practices.notes: Best-practices, 'Course-correct early and often': 'Correct Claude as soon as you notice it going off track.' The autonomy paper (anthropic.com/research/measuring-agent-autonomy, 2026-02-18) is descriptive only: users with about 10 sessions interrupt in about 5% of turns, experienced users in about 9%. It says it is 'too early to mandate specific interaction patterns'. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

suggest.name: /rewind
suggest.what: Restores code and conversation to an earlier prompt.

practices.claim: Commit or stash before risky work, because /rewind does not undo Bash file changes or subagent edits.
practices.check: A gap only when a /rewind followed Bash file changes or subagent edits and no git baseline came before them. Uncommitted work alone is not a gap.
practices.notes: Checkpointing: 'Checkpointing does not track files modified by Bash commands.' For subagents: 'rewinding doesn't restore the edits. Use git to revert them.' A foreground forked skill is the one exception. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

practices.claim: Use subagents for investigation and verbose operations so the main context gets only a short summary.
practices.check: Compare agent calls and sizes against main-context compactions. More subagents is not better; see the cost and over-spawn entries.
practices.notes: Context engineering post: subagent summaries are 'often 1,000-2,000 tokens'.

practices.claim: Multi-agent runs use about 15x the tokens of a chat, so save them for work that splits into parallel parts.
practices.check: Use cost.total split main vs subagents and agents.size. The 90.2% gain was on research evals; never claim it for coding.
practices.notes: Measured on an Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 research system: 'multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats'. The post argues, without data, that 'most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks'. The costs doc's 7x figure is for agent teams in plan mode, not subagents.

practices.claim: On Opus 4.6 and later, avoid spawning subagents for work a direct grep or read would do faster.
practices.check: Read agent calls per week and sampled prompts. A high count is a gap only if the tasks were trivial.
practices.notes: Prompting docs warn these models over-use subagents.

practices.claim: Set a model on subagent calls (for example haiku for simple ones) instead of inheriting the parent's.
practices.check: Read the explicit rate with agents.by_model. A low rate costs money only when the parent is an expensive model and the tasks are simple; inheriting is fine for hard work.
practices.notes: Costs doc recommends model: haiku for simple subagents.

practices.claim: Run several sessions in parallel, using worktrees to keep them apart.
practices.check: Worktree use and overlapping sessions show the habit. They do not show it paid off.
practices.notes: METR transcripts of 7 staff: more concurrent agents went with higher estimated time savings, but n=7 and METR calls it a soft upper bound. Boris's 'single biggest productivity unlock' posts are secondary and left out.

practices.claim: Use Sonnet for most coding and save Opus for architecture and multi-step reasoning.
practices.check: Report model mix and cost by model. Never call heavy Opus use wrong: Boris's Jan 2026 view, known only second-hand, was Opus with thinking for everything, and neither side shows data. The spend warning applies only on an API or cloud-provider plan.
practices.notes: Costs doc: 'Sonnet handles most coding tasks well and costs less than Opus. Reserve Opus for complex architectural decisions or multi-step reasoning.' And: 'Unexpectedly high spend on an API or cloud-provider plan: usually traces back to long sessions that were never cleared or to Opus left as the default model.' Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

practices.claim: Keep effort at a high setting for non-trivial coding.
practices.check: Never a gap on current models; see match-effort-to-task.
practices.notes: The postmortem covers Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6: medium effort gave 'slightly lower intelligence with significantly less latency for the majority of tasks'. The default moved from high to medium on 2026-03-04 and back on 2026-04-07. The post reverted a default; it did not tell users to keep effort high.

practices.claim: Match effort to the task: medium for clear feature work, high for bugs and edge cases, xhigh or max only when you have measured a gain.
practices.check: Describe the effort mix by model, with ultrathink and /effort counts. Raise it only as a question when most 5.5 sessions run above medium. Never flag low effort unless transcripts show the failure, such as a change reported done with no check.
practices.notes: Model-config: Opus, Sonnet and Haiku 5.5 default to medium; medium 'fits day-to-day engineering work with a clear scope, such as implementing a new feature'; high is for 'Work where verification matters or edge cases are likely, such as fixing a bug in an existing codebase'; max 'may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking'. Opus 5.5 prompting page: 'Reserve xhigh and max for work where you've measured a quality gain.' Fable 5.1 starts at high (API effort page). Opus 4.7 defaults to xhigh. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

suggest.name: /effort
suggest.what: Sets or shows the session's effort level.

practices.claim: Switching model mid-session rebuilds the cache, so weigh that cost before you switch, or hand the work to a subagent on the other model.
practices.check: Read the model_change row of cost.cache.by_cause. Look for hidden switches too: a skill's model frontmatter, opusplan, automatic fallback, fast mode. A switch is a cost trade-off, not a ban; flag it only when the rebuild cost more than the cheaper model saved.
practices.notes: Follows from pricing, not a measurement. Prompt-caching doc: 'On Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Fable 5.1 with an API key or a Claude subscription, changing effort keeps the cache'; Bedrock, Vertex and gateways can differ. Deferred MCP tools do not break the cache. Thariq, 2026-04-30 (Prompt caching is everything): switching Opus to Haiku after 100k tokens costs more than staying. At Opus 5.5 list prices that no longer holds: a cache read on 100k costs $0.02, a Haiku 5.5 5m write $0.0125.

practices.claim: The first turn after the cache expires costs 12.5x to 80x a warm turn, by model, so a pause costs least at the end of a task.
practices.check: Read the idle_over_ttl row of cost.cache.by_cause and cost.cache.waste_pct, using meta.billing.main_cache_ttl for the TTL. The TTL is a cost trade-off, never a reason to rush work or skip breaks. Breaks at a task end are normal; report mid-task gaps and what they cost.
practices.notes: Pricing page (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing): cache reads cost 0.1x input, 0.05x on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, 0.025x on Fable 5.1; 5m writes 1.25x, 1h writes 2x. So a cold turn costs 12.5x-20x a warm one at 0.1x reads, 25x-40x on Opus and Sonnet 5.5, 50x-80x on Fable 5.1. That is arithmetic, not a measurement. Main-thread TTL is 1h on a subscription within plan usage, 5m on usage credits or by default on an API key; subagents 5m by default.

suggest.name: /usage
suggest.what: Shows cache misses and flags long context or misses that take 10% or more of usage.

practices.claim: Use /rewind rather than /compact to abandon a path; compact at natural breaks, not mid-task or after the cache expires.
practices.check: Read the compaction row and /rewind use in practices.usage. A compaction that was needed to continue is not waste.
practices.notes: Documented mechanism, not a measurement. /compact on a cold cache 'reprocesses the full history as uncached input'; /rewind keeps an already-cached prefix.

practices.claim: A subagent's first request does not read the parent's cache, and subagents default to a 5-minute TTL.
practices.check: Read subagent_start_pct and what_if.subagent_ttl_1h. It is structural, so many small subagents cost more than a few large ones; do not call it a user error.
practices.notes: Documented mechanism, not a measurement. A fork does read the parent's cache.

practices.claim: Use hooks for rules that must always hold and to pre-filter large output; CLAUDE.md is only advisory.
practices.check: Hook config is not in transcripts. A gap only when transcripts show Claude breaking the same CLAUDE.md rule more than once; oversized tool results are a weaker hint.
practices.notes: Best-practices: 'Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens.' The costs doc shows a hook cutting a log read 'from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds'; an illustration, not a measurement. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

suggest.name: /hooks
suggest.what: Shows your hooks; a hook enforces a rule every time, where CLAUDE.md only asks.

practices.claim: Prefer CLI tools such as gh to MCP servers and disable unused MCP servers.
practices.check: MCP tools are now deferred by default, so the cost gap is smaller. Do not flag MCP use without evidence of definition-token cost.
practices.notes: Costs doc and best-practices call CLI the most context-efficient option; partly stale.

practices.claim: Pre-approve safe commands or use auto mode instead of clicking through prompts.
practices.check: Since v2.1.283 auto mode is the starting mode, so a session in `default` means the person chose Manual. Describe the permission-mode mix. A gap only when transcripts show long runs of approvals the person clicked through. Auto mode is 'not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure'.
practices.notes: Users approve 93% of prompts; classifier has 0.4% false positives (n=10,000) and 17% false negatives (n=52) on real overeager actions. Best-practices: 'With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, auto mode is the built-in starting permission mode' for terminal and VS Code sessions.

practices.claim: When the same safe command keeps prompting, allow it once in settings instead of approving it each time.
practices.check: Triage by command shape; a gap only when the same shape repeats. Repeated read_only commands: suggest /fewer-permission-prompts. Allowed commands denied for how they were written (chained, absolute_path, inline_interpreter such as python -c): report the pattern; the fix is instructions, not more rules. Never suggest blanket interpreter, shell or network allowlists.
practices.notes: Best-practices, 'Configure permissions': 'After the tenth approval you're clicking through rather than reviewing.' It advises allowlists for 'specific tools you know are safe, like npm run lint or git commit', and sandboxing. Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

suggest.name: /fewer-permission-prompts
suggest.what: Scans your transcripts for repeated read-only commands and adds them to the project allowlist.

practices.claim: Use bypassPermissions only in an isolated container or VM.
practices.check: Transcripts cannot show isolation. When bypass sessions appear, name them and ask whether they ran in a container or VM; never call them a gap on the count alone.
practices.notes: Permission-modes table: bypassPermissions is best for 'Isolated containers and VMs only'. It 'disables permission prompts and safety checks so tool calls execute immediately, including writes to protected paths.' Date is the fetch date; docs are undated.

practices.claim: People misjudge their own AI speed-up, so trust only measured time savings with stated methods, never self-reports.
practices.check: Never report hours saved from self-reports or from transcripts. Cite a time saving only from a measured study that states its method; otherwise report process signals.
practices.notes: RCT, 16 developers: forecast 24% faster, believed 20% faster, measured 19% slower. Claude 3.x era, and the blog calls its results out of date. Unvalidated self-reports are not evidence; measured time estimates with stated methods are, such as METR's 2026 transcript notes, which METR calls a soft upper bound.

practices.claim: More code or merged PRs does not mean better outcomes; complexity and warnings can rise with it.
practices.check: Do not praise lines written or sessions run. Prefer rework signals.
practices.notes: Found a transient velocity gain with a persistent rise in static-analysis warnings and complexity; Cursor, not Claude Code.

practices.claim: Avoid CRITICAL/MUST shouting in prompts and CLAUDE.md; emphasize one line at most.
practices.check: A count of emphasis words in CLAUDE.md is a hint only. A gap only when transcripts show Claude over-applying an emphasized rule.
practices.notes: Prompting docs: dial back aggressive language on these models; it 'may now overtrigger'. The one-line advice is on best-practices (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices): 'add emphasis such as "IMPORTANT" to that line alone. If you emphasize many lines, none of them stands out.'

practices.claim: Have Claude read the files it will touch, copy existing patterns and check which imports the project already uses before writing code; if no pattern exists, it should ask.
practices.check: No metric. A sample reader can check whether edits to a file were preceded by a read of it or of a neighbour; a gap only where samples show the person correcting style or conventions.
practices.notes: Gist section I (Read Before You Write). Opinion of a respected practitioner (gist 'CLAUDE.md: Field Notes on Getting a Language Model to Write Code You Will Not Rewrite', posted under DiTo97; original post https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876), not Anthropic advice and not measured. Date is the fetch date.

practices.claim: Have Claude state its assumptions and tradeoffs before coding, and ask when the request is unclear instead of filling the gap with plausible-looking code.
practices.check: No metric. Read it from sample readers: corrections where Claude guessed an unclear requirement. Overlaps course-correct-early, which is about the person's timing.
practices.notes: Gist section II (Think Before You Code). Opinion of a respected practitioner (gist 'CLAUDE.md: Field Notes on Getting a Language Model to Write Code You Will Not Rewrite', posted under DiTo97; original post https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876), not Anthropic advice and not measured. Date is the fetch date.

practices.claim: Ask for the minimum code that solves the problem: no premature abstraction, unneeded error handling or configuration nobody asked for.
practices.check: No metric. A sample reader can look for corrections that reject over-engineering. Not measurable from diff size.
practices.notes: Gist section III (Simplicity) and the 'Wrong Abstraction' failure mode in section X. Opinion of a respected practitioner (gist 'CLAUDE.md: Field Notes on Getting a Language Model to Write Code You Will Not Rewrite', posted under DiTo97; original post https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876), not Anthropic advice and not measured. Date is the fetch date.

practices.claim: Keep diffs minimal: every changed line traces to the request, match the existing style, and do no drive-by reformatting or restructuring of unrelated code.
practices.check: No metric. Read it only from sample readers, never from the number of changed files; a gap only when samples show the person rejecting or reverting unrelated edits. Related to respect-task-scope, which covers added work on newer models.
practices.notes: Gist section IV (Surgical Changes) and the 'Kitchen Sink' and 'Runaway Refactor' failure modes in section X. Opinion of a respected practitioner (gist 'CLAUDE.md: Field Notes on Getting a Language Model to Write Code You Will Not Rewrite', posted under DiTo97; original post https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876), not Anthropic advice and not measured. Date is the fetch date.

practices.claim: For a bug, reproduce it with a failing test first, watch it fail, then fix the cause rather than the symptom (find out why a value is null instead of adding a null check); change one thing at a time.
practices.check: No metric: verification.check_after_last_edit shows a check ran after the last edit, not that a test failed first. A sample reader can look at whether bug-fix sessions reproduced before editing.
practices.notes: Gist sections V (Verification) and VII (Debugging). Opinion of a respected practitioner (gist 'CLAUDE.md: Field Notes on Getting a Language Model to Write Code You Will Not Rewrite', posted under DiTo97; original post https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876), not Anthropic advice and not measured. Date is the fetch date.

practices.claim: Prefer the standard library or a dependency the project already has; require a stated reason for each new dependency.
practices.check: No metric. A sample reader can check whether a session added a package without discussing it; nothing counts dependency changes.
practices.notes: Gist section VIII (Dependencies): 'every dependency is code you don't control'. Opinion of a respected practitioner (gist 'CLAUDE.md: Field Notes on Getting a Language Model to Write Code You Will Not Rewrite', posted under DiTo97; original post https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876), not Anthropic advice and not measured. Date is the fetch date.
